sections.title: How to use this toolkit
sections.html:
This is a self-study chapter for the first session. Work through the five numbered sections in order. First identify the decision and define what would count as success. Then inspect the evidence, reproduce a small calculation in Excel 365 and SPSS, and write a bounded recommendation. The Try it questions are ungraded; attempt each before reading its answer.

The course has no required textbook. The supplied crosswalk headings from Albright and Winston, Field, and Knaflic are scope cues, not a claim that you have read those chapters. Core cues here concern the role of business analytics, spreadsheet practice, and getting oriented in SPSS. Measurement, research design, and communication headings serve as brief optional bridges. This chapter is an original synthesis grounded in the open and primary sources actually cited below; its case and exercises are fictional and original.

This source has no stable PDF page numbers. Future slides, speaker notes, PNP materials, or paginated versions should cross-reference stable numbered section headings such as §3.2, then add page numbers after pagination. Later sessions develop displays, distributions, probability, sampling, tests, and regression. Those methods are signposts here, not prerequisites.

sections.title: The running case: Cedar Cup pickup orders
sections.short: The running case: Cedar Cup pick…
sections.html:
Cedar Cup is entirely fictional. Its campus café manager is deciding whether to pilot a staffed handoff point for mobile pickup orders. The manager worries that customers reach the counter but do not receive their drinks promptly. The stakeholder is the manager, who controls staffing; customers and staff are also affected stakeholders.

Define the population of interest as all Cedar Cup mobile pickup orders placed during a proposed two-week pilot, rather than all café purchases. Exclude canceled orders only under a rule stated before analysis. An order does not become ineligible merely because a timestamp is missing. The unit of analysis is one order. Eight orders from two recent morning shifts form a small, conveniently selected readiness extract—not a random sample of the proposed pilot population. Each order_id should identify one order. Waiting time is handoff time minus recorded arrival time, in minutes. “Within five minutes” means at most five minutes, including exactly five. Report missing outcomes separately and predefine how they affect any all-order KPI.

Order IDMorning shiftWait (minutes)Within 5 minutes?
C101Tuesday21
C102Tuesday41
C103Tuesday60
C104Tuesday80
C105Wednesday31
C106Wednesday51
C107Wednesday70
C108Wednesday90

These eight rows are the checked analysis table. The illustrative source export initially contained nine rows because it repeated C104. An analyst confirmed that the second C104 row was a duplicate export record, retained one source record, and documented that decision. Never remove repeated IDs automatically: two genuine events could require a different data definition.

Observed evidence: four of eight checked orders met the five-minute definition. Limitations: the extract covers only two mornings; recorded arrival may differ from when a customer actually reached the pickup point; and it contains no handoff-point pilot or labor-cost observations. It can describe these eight orders. It cannot estimate the intervention’s effect or prove its cost is acceptable.

sections.title: 1. Turn a concern into a decision question
sections.short: 1. Turn a concern into a decisio…
sections.html: Why these scores: A precise decision, measure, and claim determine whether any subsequent analysis is useful.

sections.title: 1.1 Stakeholder, action, KPI, target, and guardrail
sections.html:
“Pickup is slow” is a managerial concern, not yet an analysis question. A usable question names the action and the evidence that would inform it: Should Cedar Cup keep the staffed handoff point after a defined two-week pilot? The KPI (key performance indicator) is the proportion of eligible mobile pickup orders handed over within five minutes of recorded arrival. Its unit is a percentage of orders, not minutes or customers. A target says what result the manager seeks: at least 75% within five minutes. A guardrail limits an unwanted trade-off: additional handoff labor cost no greater than $1.50 per eligible order. These thresholds are fictional planning choices, not established industry benchmarks.

Write the denominator and boundary rule before calculating a rate. Here, each eligible order enters the denominator once, and a five-minute wait counts as meeting the KPI.

Work the baseline by hand. The eight waits are 2, 4, 6, 8, 3, 5, 7, and 9 minutes. Four—2, 4, 3, and 5—are at most five. Therefore:

Observed within-five-minute rate=4 eligible orders within five minutes8 eligible orders=0.50=50%.\text{Observed within-five-minute rate} =\frac{4\text{ eligible orders within five minutes}} {8\text{ eligible orders}} =0.50=50\%.

The observed rate is 25 percentage points below the 75% target: 75%−50%=2575\%-50\%=25 percentage points. Reaching 75% among eight orders would require six successes, or two more than observed. That arithmetic does not say the proposed staffing change will produce two extra successes.

A testable claim for the proposed pilot is: During the two-week pilot, the eligible-order KPI will be at least 75%, while additional handoff labor cost will be at most $1.50 per eligible order. To test it, the team must define pilot dates, count every eligible order under the same time rule, and record incremental labor cost. A claim about improvement caused by staffing needs a credible comparison design as well; a before-and-after difference alone can reflect changes in demand or shift conditions. Distinguishing observational evidence from an intervention is central to sound research design (Illowsky & Dean, 2023b).

Failure mode: Reporting “four fast pickups” without the eight-order denominator, or silently changing “within five” to “under five,” changes the meaning of the evidence. Calling 50% “the pilot result” is also wrong: no pilot has occurred in the case.

Try it — ungraded. In the same eight-order extract, suppose the manager instead defines success as under five minutes. What rate results, and why is this not the original KPI?

Explained answer. Only waits of 2, 3, and 4 are under five. The rate becomes 3/8=0.375=37.5%3/8=0.375=37.5\%. The five-minute order changes category. This is a new boundary rule, not a recalculation of the previously agreed “at most five” KPI.

sections.title: 1.2 Define the population and the evidence needed
sections.html:
A population is the complete set of units to which a claim is meant to apply; a sample is the units actually observed. In this case, the proposed two-week pilot’s eligible mobile pickup orders are the decision population. The eight historical orders are observed units from a different period. A variable records a property of each unit: wait_min is quantitative, whereas within_5 is a categorical yes/no outcome coded 1 or 0. Giving categories numeric codes does not turn them into measured minutes. These distinctions help prevent a convenient extract from being mistaken for the full population (Illowsky & Dean, 2023a).

For a complete example, suppose the pilot later records 40 eligible orders, 30 within five minutes, and $48 in additional handoff labor. The KPI would be 30/40=75%30/40=75\%. Additional cost per eligible order would be $48/40=$1.20\$48/40=\$1.20. Those invented pilot figures would meet both stated thresholds for those 40 orders. They would not, by themselves, establish that staffing caused the result: day, volume, and order mix might differ. The calculation also depends on using the same 40 eligible orders as each denominator. This hypothetical calculation is practice, not a second observed Cedar Cup dataset.

Failure mode: Using all café transactions to divide a count of timely mobile pickups makes the rate artificially small. Conversely, excluding inconvenient eligible orders without a documented rule can make it look artificially large.

Try it — ungraded. A manager reports 12 timely handoffs among 15 orders with timestamps. There were also three mobile orders whose arrival times were not recorded. Can you report “12 of 18 within five minutes”?

Explained answer. No. All 18 mobile orders remain eligible, but three outcomes are unknown under this definition. Report 12 of 15 timestamp-complete orders, or 80% among measured orders, alongside three eligible orders with missing measurement. Investigate why they are missing and apply a prespecified missing-outcome rule before claiming a rate for all 18.

sections.title: 2. Check what each row means
sections.html: Why these scores: A correct formula cannot repair duplicated units, missing timestamps, or an undocumented export.

sections.title: 2.1 Grain, provenance, and measurement checks
sections.html:
Grain means what one row represents. The checked Cedar Cup table has one row per eligible order. Its key is order_id. Provenance is the record of where data came from and how they changed: for example, a dated mobile-order export, the timestamp fields used, the duplicate C104 investigation, and the resulting checked table. Keep the unchanged source export separately from the analysis copy. This makes a correction inspectable rather than invisible.

Before opening software, set out the calculation. Let arrival_time and handoff_time be recorded clock times for the same order. Compute wait_min as their difference in minutes, provided both exist and handoff follows arrival. Then set within_5 to 1 if 0≤wait_min≤50\leq\text{wait\_min}\leq5, otherwise 0 for a valid wait. For C106, an arrival at 09:10 and handoff at 09:15 give 09:15−09:10=509{:}15-09{:}10=5 minutes, so within_5 = 1. If arrival is blank, the outcome is missing, not 0. Confirm timestamp time zones and whether an order can cross a date boundary before calculating a larger file.

Validate the unit count independently of the KPI. The initial export has nine rows but eight distinct order IDs. Investigating the repeated C104 yields eight checked orders; counting its extra export row as another order would change the denominator without adding a customer decision unit.

A compact check record for this case is:

CheckExpected in this teaching extractIf it fails
Checked rows8Reconcile additions or exclusions
Distinct order_id values8Inspect repeated keys against source events
Valid, nonmissing waits8Investigate timestamp coverage and ordering
within_5 successes4Recheck the five-minute boundary and calculations

The extract’s two mornings are convenient, not randomly chosen. Even perfectly entered values could poorly represent evenings, busy days, or the proposed pilot. Selection and measurement problems are different: correcting C104 addresses duplication but not generalizability. Sampling and data variation are developed later in the course (Illowsky & Dean, 2023a).

Failure mode: “Remove duplicates” is not a complete cleaning rule. A repeated order ID might represent an erroneous repeated export, two status events, or an ID-system defect. Determine which occurred and preserve the decision trail.

Try it — ungraded. Suppose the source has one additional row for C109, but its handoff timestamp is blank. Should C109 be coded within_5 = 0?

Explained answer. No. A missing handoff timestamp does not establish a wait longer than five minutes. Mark its outcome missing, report the missing-record count, and investigate it. A policy for eligible orders with missing outcomes must be stated before using their data in a performance claim.

sections.title: 3. Reproduce the small result in Excel 365
sections.html: Why these scores: A small, auditable workbook is a practical readiness check and a foundation for later analyses.

sections.title: 3.1 Set up the workbook and calculate the rate
sections.short: 3.1. Set up the workbook and cal…
sections.html:
Start with inputs, units, and expected result. Enter the eight checked rows in columns order_id, shift, and wait_min; create an empty within_5 column for a formula. wait_min uses minutes; within_5 will use 1 for yes and 0 for no. Expect eight orders, four successes, and 4/8=50%4/8=50\%. Keep a separate note identifying the source export and the C104 resolution. Do not type over the original export.

In Excel 365, select the four headers, three populated input columns, and eight rows; create an Excel table named Pickup, leaving within_5 cells blank. Tables support structured references such as Pickup[wait_min], which identify a column by name and adjust when table rows change (Microsoft, n.d.-a). Enter this formula in the first data cell under within_5 and confirm Excel fills the calculated column:

=IF([@wait_min]<=5,1,0)

[@wait_min] means the wait in this row. IF returns 1 when the condition is true and 0 otherwise. With the eight already validated, nonnegative, nonmissing waits supplied here, the results are 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0. This formula is not a safe missing-value policy for an unclean file: validate waits and handle missing inputs explicitly before extending it.

Calculate outside the table:

=COUNT(Pickup[wait_min])
=SUM(Pickup[within_5])
=SUM(Pickup[within_5])/COUNT(Pickup[wait_min])

The first formula returns 8 numeric waits; the second returns 4 successes; the third returns 0.5, displayed as 50% when formatted as a percentage. COUNT here checks how many waits are numeric; it is an appropriate denominator only because all eight checked eligible orders have valid waits. If that check fails, stop and resolve eligibility and missingness rather than quietly changing the denominator.

Make an independent check with a different route:

=COUNTIF(Pickup[wait_min],"<=5")

It should return 4. COUNTIF counts cells meeting one stated condition (Microsoft, n.d.-b). Check that COUNTIF’s four agrees with SUM’s four, then inspect C106’s boundary value of five by eye. Agreement is reassuring, but two formulas can share a mistaken definition; the written KPI is the final check.

Failure mode: A percentage formatted as 50% may conceal a bad denominator. If nine exported rows include the duplicate C104, a formula over that range answers a different question. Verify the grain and row count before trusting the display.

Try it — ungraded. After checking the source, an analyst corrects C103’s wait from six minutes to five. What should the success count and rate become for the same eight orders?

Explained answer. C103 changes from 0 to 1 because five meets “at most five.” Successes become 4+1=54+1=5; the denominator remains eight; 5/8=0.625=62.5%5/8=0.625=62.5\%. The 12.5-percentage-point change from a one-minute correction shows why boundary records merit attention. It does not make the intervention effective.

sections.title: 3.2 Make the workbook inspectable
sections.html:
Separate raw source, checked order table, and summary in clearly named sheets or files. Add a short readme giving the as-of date, who supplied the export, the unit, definitions, the C104 decision, and unresolved questions. Preserve formulas so another analyst can trace 50% back to four individual orders. A spreadsheet is a model when its inputs, rules, and outputs encode a business question—not merely when it has many formulas.

For example, a reviewer can trace C106 through wait_min = 5, within_5 = 1, the success sum of 4, and the denominator of 8. Then the reviewer can independently count the four waits at or below five in the source table. If a later export has 80 rows, that same trail should reveal whether the added rows are eligible and whether the definitions stayed fixed. Structured references can make expanding tables easier, but they do not validate the new rows for you (Microsoft, n.d.-a).

Failure mode: Pasting a screenshot of “50%” into a presentation without the definition, count, and source date makes it hard to audit or responsibly reuse. Do not put customer identifiers in a broadly shared presentation merely because they appear in an operational export.

Try it — ungraded. Which is the stronger summary label: “Pickup success: 50%” or “4 of 8 checked mobile pickup orders handed over within five minutes; two morning shifts”? Explain.

Explained answer. The second states the count, denominator, rule, and coverage. The first could be mistaken for an all-orders, all-hours, or pilot-wide result.

sections.title: 4. Get oriented in SPSS without losing the question
sections.html: Why these scores: Tool readiness matters, but knowing where results came from matters more than memorizing menus.

sections.title: 4.1 Import, inspect, and produce one check
sections.html:
Before tool clicks, know the input: eight checked order rows, with order_id as an identifier, shift as a category, wait_min in minutes, and within_5 as 0/1. The expected frequency output is four 0s and four 1s; the business interpretation is four of eight within five minutes. The Excel result supplies an independent comparison, not a reason to ignore SPSS warnings.

Save a copy of the checked table as an Excel workbook with one header row. In SPSS, use File → Import Data → Excel, choose the intended worksheet, and set the first row as variable names. IBM notes that the first worksheet is read by default unless another is selected, so inspect the choice before proceeding (IBM, n.d.-a). In Data View, check eight cases—SPSS’s term for rows—and inspect C106. In Variable View, check names, types, labels, missing-value settings, and measurement levels. Set the order ID as a string identifier; describe shift and within_5 as categorical, and wait_min as a numeric minute measure. Variable View stores these descriptions with the data file (IBM, n.d.-b).

For a reproducible check, open a Syntax Editor and run this command against the active checked dataset:

FREQUENCIES VARIABLES=within_5.

Read it one step at a time: FREQUENCIES requests counts; VARIABLES=within_5 selects the outcome column; the period ends the SPSS command. Expect 0: four cases; 1: four cases; valid total: eight. Divide the count coded 1 by the valid total: 4/8=50%4/8=50\%. The Viewer holds the resulting table; it is output, not the underlying data. IBM documents both the distinct Data Editor, Viewer, and Syntax Editor roles and the FREQUENCIES command (IBM, n.d.-c, n.d.-d).

Failure mode: An import can look successful while reading the wrong worksheet or interpreting a code as text. A frequency table showing only seven valid outcomes calls for investigation, not immediate celebration that the software “ran.”

Try it — ungraded. SPSS shows four 1s, three 0s, and one missing within_5. Does its “50% of all eight cases” match the originally checked dataset?

Explained answer. No. The original dataset has four 1s and four 0s, with no missing outcomes. Although 4/8=50%4/8=50\% uses eight cases, 4/7≈57.1%4/7\approx57.1\% of the seven valid outcomes gives another possible percentage. Neither discrepancy should be accepted until the missing value and import are reconciled against the checked eight rows.

sections.title: 4.2 Save distinct data, syntax, and output artifacts
sections.html:
SPSS has several artifacts with different purposes. Save the data file so the checked cases and variable definitions can be reopened; save the syntax so a colleague can rerun the frequency request; save the Viewer output so a colleague can inspect what that run displayed. If an accessible report is needed, export selected output and also supply its small count table as text. An exported image alone is not a substitute for data and syntax. IBM describes saving SPSS data with its variable dictionary and exporting Viewer output to other formats (IBM, n.d.-e, n.d.-f).

For this case, sensible names might be cedar_checked_orders.sav, cedar_readiness.sps, and cedar_readiness_output.spv. Reopen the saved data and rerun the syntax. The check succeeds if the Viewer again reports four zeros, four ones, eight valid cases. Record the extract date and duplicate decision outside the numeric output. Never use the sample file names as evidence that customer-level data are approved for unrestricted sharing.

Failure mode: Saving only the output preserves a result without a reliable route back to its inputs. Saving only data preserves inputs without documenting which result was produced or how.

Try it — ungraded. A teammate sends an output screenshot reading “50%” and a syntax file, but no checked data or source description. What can you verify?

Explained answer. You can inspect what the syntax asks SPSS to calculate and read the displayed number. You cannot rerun it or verify the eight rows, eligibility rule, C104 correction, or provenance. Request the appropriately shareable checked data and its source-and-cleaning record.

sections.title: 5. Communicate a bounded next step
sections.html: Why these scores: Managers need a decision-ready statement that separates what was seen from what is proposed.

sections.title: 5.1 Observation, inference, assumption, recommendation
sections.html:
Use four labels to prevent a small extract from carrying a claim it cannot support.

  • Descriptive observation: In the eight checked orders from two morning shifts, four met the five-minute rule: 50%.
  • Inference: The extract does not establish the rate for all future eligible orders. A population claim needs an appropriate sampling or study plan; that work begins in later sessions.
  • Assumption to check: Recorded arrival is a useful start time for customer waiting, and the proposed staff member can be assigned without unacceptable disruption elsewhere.
  • Recommendation: Do not approve permanent staffing from this extract alone. Prepare a time-bounded pilot that records eligibility, waits, source quality, and incremental labor cost, then evaluate its target and guardrail.

This is a bounded recommendation: it says what to do next without claiming that the staffed point works. For the pilot, predefine the date range and treatment, keep the five-minute boundary fixed, log all eligible orders and missing timestamps, and compare like with like where feasible. Consider effects on staff workload and on customers who do not use mobile pickup. Later units address uncertainty, comparison designs, practical effects, and A/B guardrails in depth; a “statistically significant” result, even if one were calculated, would not alone prove causal or business impact (Illowsky & Dean, 2023b).

Lead with the decision and its evidential boundary, not an unqualified percentage. A suitable manager-facing line is: “Two checked morning shifts show 4 of 8 mobile pickups handed over within five minutes; this is a reason to measure a pilot, not evidence that extra staffing will fix the delay.”

A compact text display can carry the present evidence without relying on color:

Checked morning ordersWithin 5 minutesOver 5 minutesWhat it supports
84 (50%)4 (50%)Description of these checked orders only

For a later chart, label categories and counts directly and accompany it with the data table or equivalent text. Do not make its visual emphasis imply that an intervention effect was measured. Protect operational identifiers when sharing beyond the authorized team.

Failure mode: “Staffing will lift pickup performance from 50% to 75%” converts a target into a forecast without evidence. “Most customers waited too long” is also unsupported: the unit here is orders, and four of eight—not most—exceeded five minutes.

Try it — ungraded. Rewrite this sentence for a manager: “Our data prove the staffed point will hit the target because the baseline is 50%.”

Explained answer. One sound version is: “In two checked morning shifts, 4 of 8 eligible orders met the five-minute rule. We have not observed a staffed handoff point, so we recommend a measured pilot before deciding whether to retain one.” It retains the useful observation and removes the unsupported causal prediction.

sections.title: Recap
sections.html:
• Define the stakeholder and decision before choosing a method.
  • State the population, one-row unit, eligibility rule, and denominator.
  • A KPI needs an exact boundary: Cedar Cup’s “within five minutes” includes five.
  • Separate a desired target from an observed result and a cost guardrail.
  • In the checked fictional extract, 4/8=50%4/8=50\%; it describes eight orders, not a staffing effect.
  • Trace source rows, keys, missing values, and corrections before calculating.
  • Check Excel’s answer by another calculation and against individual rows.
  • In SPSS, distinguish data, syntax, and Viewer output; save what another analyst needs to rerun the check.
  • Tell managers what was observed, what remains uncertain, and the next defensible action.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
• Case: SPSS term for an observed row; here, one checked order.
  • Categorical variable: A recorded group or class; shift is Tuesday or Wednesday.
  • Convenience extract: Readily available observations not selected by a probability rule; the eight orders were pulled from two mornings.
  • Denominator: The count of eligible units used beneath a rate; eight checked orders in the baseline calculation.
  • Grain: What one row represents; one eligible order in this table.
  • Guardrail: A limit on a possible downside of a decision; at most $1.50 additional labor per eligible order.
  • Inference: A claim extending beyond observed units; the eight orders alone do not justify a pilot-wide rate.
  • Key: A field intended to identify a unit uniquely; order_id should identify one order.
  • KPI: A specified measure of performance; the share of eligible orders handed over within five minutes.
  • Measurement rule: The operational way a value is obtained; wait is recorded handoff time minus recorded arrival time.
  • Missing value: An outcome that cannot be determined from available data; a blank arrival time does not mean failure.
  • Population: All units the intended claim concerns; here, eligible orders during the proposed two-week pilot.
  • Provenance: A record of data origin and changes; the export source and C104 resolution are part of it.
  • Sample: Units observed rather than the whole population; the historical eight orders are not the proposed pilot population.
  • Stakeholder: A person affected by or responsible for a decision; the café manager, customers, and staff qualify.
  • Target: A desired KPI level; at least 75% within five minutes.
  • Testable claim: A statement with defined observations that could support or contradict it; the pilot target plus labor guardrail.
  • Variable: A property recorded for each unit; wait_min records minutes for each checked order.
